lessons.title: der/die/das and ein/eine — "the" and "a"
lessons.summary: German never lets a noun stand alone: it needs "the" or "a" in front — except in the plural, where "a" simply does not exist.
lessons.rule:
Turkish has no word for the and no word for a. German has six of them, and you cannot leave them out. Almost every German noun walks around with one of these little words in front of it.

Every noun has a gender. This is not about male and female in any real sense — it is a label glued to the word, and you learn it together with the word. Masculine nouns take der, feminine nouns take die, neuter nouns take das. So never learn Tisch. Learn der Tisch.

der/die/das means "the" — the one we both already know about. ein/eine means "a" — any one of them, or one you are mentioning for the first time. Da ist ein Café. (you don't know it yet) becomes Das Café ist neu. (now you do).

Two traps for you. First: eine is only for feminine nouns. Masculine and neuter both use plain ein — ein Mann, ein Kind. Second, and bigger: ein has no plural form at all. There is no "eine Bücher". The plural of ein Buch is simply Bücher, with nothing in front of it.

The plural is the one easy part of the whole system: every plural noun takes die as its "the", whatever gender it had in the singular. der Mann → die Männer, das Kind → die Kinder, die Lampe → die Lampen.

tables.title: Same noun: first mention, then after that

examples.de: Da ist ein Café. Das Café ist neu.
examples.en: There's a café. The café is new.
examples.note: First mention → ein. Second mention, we both know which one → das.
Frage is feminine, so it gets eine. You will say this sentence a lot at work.

examples.de: Der Mann dort ist mein Nachbar.
examples.en: The man over there is my neighbour.
examples.note: Mann is masculine → der. "dort" shows we mean one specific man, so it's definite.
Plural with no article at all. "eine Äpfel" does not exist in German.
Every plural takes die, even though the singular is das Buch.

mistakes.why: Auto is neuter (das Auto), and neuter takes plain ein. Only feminine nouns get eine.
ein/eine has no plural form. In the plural you use no article at all.
Turkish has no articles, so dropping them feels natural. In German a countable noun almost always needs der/die/das or ein/eine in front of it.
Gender belongs to the word, not to the object. You have to memorise Handy together with das.

drills.question: ___ Mann ist mein Nachbar.
drills.explain: Mann is a masculine noun, and masculine "the" is der.

drills.question: Ich habe ___ Frage.
drills.explain: Frage is feminine, and feminine is the only gender that takes eine.

drills.question: Das ist ___ Auto. (a — das Auto)
drills.explain: Neuter uses the same short form as masculine, so it is ein and never eine.
The article sits directly in front of its noun, and the verb takes second position.

drills.question: Which sentence is correct?
drills.explain: There is no plural of ein, so a plural noun mentioned for the first time gets nothing in front of it.

drills.question: Da ist ein Café. ___ Café ist neu. (the)
drills.explain: On the second mention we both know which café, so it switches from ein to the definite article.

drills.question: ___ Bücher sind teuer.
drills.explain: All plurals take die, no matter what the singular gender was.

drills.answer: Ich suche eine Wohnung in Berlin
drills.explain: Wohnung is feminine and you have not named a specific one yet, so it is eine.

lessons.title: Saying no: kein vs nicht
lessons.summary: German has two words for "not": kein cancels a noun, nicht cancels everything else — and nicht has its own place in the sentence.
lessons.rule:
In Turkish you glue the negative onto the verb (gelmiyorum) or add değil. German makes you pick between two different words: kein and nicht. Picking the wrong one is the single most common beginner mistake there is.

kein cancels a noun. A noun is a thing-word: Auto, Zeit, Geld, Hunger. Here is the test: look at what stands in front of the noun. If it is ein/eine, or if there is nothing there, use kein. Ich habe ein Auto → Ich habe kein Auto. Ich habe Zeit → Ich habe keine Zeit. kein takes exactly the same endings as ein.

nicht cancels everything else — verbs (Ich fahre nicht), adjectives, which are describing words like teuer or müde (nicht teuer), places (nicht in Berlin), names (Das ist nicht Emre), and any noun that already has der/die/das or mein/dein in front of it. That slot is taken, so kein cannot get in.

Where does nicht stand? Directly in front of whatever it is aiming at: before an adjective, before a place, before a second verb at the end of the sentence. If there is nothing to aim at, it drops to the very end: Ich arbeite heute nicht. It never goes between the subject and the verb.

One thing early, because you will need it every day: when the noun is the thing being acted on, masculine kein becomes keinen — Ich habe keinen Hunger. Feminine, neuter and plural stay unchanged. The case lessons will explain why; for now just learn the phrase.

tables.title: kein takes the same endings as ein
Which word do I use?
headers: What stands in front of the noun
rows: no noun — a verb or adjective

tables.title: Where nicht goes
rows: A second verb at the end

examples.note: You could have said "ein Auto", so the negative word is kein.
Zeit had no article in front of it, and that is still kein territory. Zeit is feminine → keine.
There is no noun to cancel, so nicht falls to the end of the sentence.
nicht stands right in front of the describing word it cancels.
mein already fills the slot in front of the noun, so kein is impossible here.
Hunger is masculine and is the thing being had, so kein takes the extra -en.

mistakes.why: Zeit is a noun with nothing in front of it — exactly the situation kein is made for. This is the most frequent negation error of all.
A noun gets only one word in front of it. mein is already there, so you must negate with nicht.
nicht never squeezes in between the subject and the verb. The verb stays in second position and nicht goes to the end.
When there is a place in the sentence, nicht goes in front of it. Only with nothing to aim at does nicht land at the very end.

drills.question: Ich habe ___ Auto.
drills.explain: Auto is a noun that could have taken ein, so it is cancelled with kein — and neuter adds no ending.

drills.question: Ich habe ___ Zeit.
drills.explain: A bare noun with no article still belongs to kein, and Zeit is feminine so it takes -e.

drills.question: Das ist ___ mein Handy.
drills.explain: mein is already sitting in front of the noun, which blocks kein completely.

drills.question: Ich arbeite heute ___. (not)
drills.explain: There is no adjective, place or noun to aim at, so nicht goes to the end.
nicht stands immediately before the describing word it cancels, not after it.

drills.question: Danke, ich habe ___ Hunger.
drills.explain: Hunger is masculine and it is the thing being had, which is where kein grows the ending -en.
A place phrase pulls nicht in front of it instead of leaving it at the end.

drills.question: Ich kann heute ___ kommen. (not)
drills.explain: When a second verb waits at the end of the sentence, nicht slots in just before it.

lessons.title: ich, du, er, sie, es — and Sie
lessons.summary: The words for I, you, he, she, it, we and they — plus the du/Sie choice that Germans genuinely notice.
lessons.rule:
A pronoun is a short stand-in word so you don't have to repeat a name. Instead of Emre kommt aus der Türkei you say er kommt aus der Türkei. These are the subject pronouns: the person or thing doing the action.

Careful with es. English says "it" for every object. German does not — it follows the noun's gender instead. Wo ist der Schlüssel? — Er ist hier. Wo ist die Rechnung? — Sie ist hier. Only das-nouns turn into es.

Three different sie. sie = she, sie = they, Sie = formal you. The formal one is always written with a capital S, even in the middle of a sentence. Apart from that, the verb ending tells you which is which: sie wohnt (she), sie wohnen (they), Sie wohnen (you, formal). Spoken aloud, sie wohnen and Sie wohnen sound identical — only the situation tells you.

du or Sie? Turkish has sen and siz, so the idea is familiar, but Germany draws the line harder and keeps it much longer. Sie is the safe default with anyone you don't know: shop staff, waiters, your landlord, the Bürgeramt, a doctor, an older neighbour, a new colleague in a traditional company. du is for friends, family, children, teenagers, students — and most IT teams, where du is normal from the first day.

Do not switch to du on your own. The offer comes from the older or more senior person (Wir können uns duzen or Sag doch du), and then you take it. Using du too early is one of the very few language mistakes Germans really do react to.

tables.title: The personal pronouns (subject form)
rows: you — one person you know well
you — several people you know well
you — formal, one person or many

tables.title: du or Sie in real life
rows: A stranger, shop staff, a waiter
Default for anyone you don't know.
An older neighbour in the building
A new colleague in a classic company
Your dev team in a tech company
Most IT workplaces are du from day one.
That is the offer. Accept it and switch.

examples.de: Ich heiße Emre und ich komme aus der Türkei.
examples.en: My name is Emre and I come from Turkey.
examples.note: ich is written small in the middle of a sentence, unlike English "I".
To a stranger or an official: capital S, verb ending -en.
The same question to a friend. du has its own verb ending, -st.

examples.de: Wo ist der Schlüssel? — Er ist hier.
examples.en: Where is the key? — It's here.
examples.note: Schlüssel is a der-noun, so it becomes er. German follows gender, not the English "it".
The -t ending shows this is one person: she, not they.
ihr is for two or more people you would each call du — a couple of friends, for example.

mistakes.wrong: Wie heißt du? — to the clerk at the Bürgeramt
mistakes.right: Wie heißen Sie? — to the clerk at the Bürgeramt
mistakes.why: du with a stranger or an official sounds rude in Germany, even when you mean it warmly. Start with Sie every time.

mistakes.wrong: Ich komme aus der Türkei und Ich wohne in Berlin.
mistakes.right: Ich komme aus der Türkei und ich wohne in Berlin.
mistakes.why: German capitalises nouns, not ich. The only pronoun with a capital letter mid-sentence is formal Sie.

mistakes.wrong: Wo ist die Rechnung? Es ist auf dem Tisch.
mistakes.right: Wo ist die Rechnung? Sie ist auf dem Tisch.
mistakes.why: English uses "it" for every object; German picks er, sie or es from the noun's gender. Rechnung is a die-noun, so it is sie.

mistakes.wrong: Meine Kollegen sind nett. Sie wohnt in Berlin.
mistakes.right: Meine Kollegen sind nett. Sie wohnen in Berlin.
mistakes.why: sie meaning "they" always takes the -en ending. The verb ending, not the pronoun, tells people how many.

drills.question: ___ heiße Emre.
drills.explain: The verb ending -e on heiße belongs to ich and to nobody else.

drills.question: Wie heißen ___? (you're at the Bürgeramt)
drills.explain: An official you have never met always gets the formal Sie.

drills.question: Wo wohnst ___? (your friend Ali)
drills.explain: The verb ending -st only ever pairs with du, and a friend gets du anyway.

drills.question: Wo ist der Schlüssel? ___ ist hier. (it)
drills.explain: Schlüssel is a der-noun, so the stand-in word is er even though English says "it".

drills.question: Wo ist die Rechnung? ___ ist auf dem Tisch. (it)
drills.explain: A die-noun is replaced by sie — gender decides the pronoun, not whether it's a person.
wir takes the -en ending, and the verb stays in second position.
In a question the verb comes first, and formal Sie keeps its capital letter and its -en ending.

drills.question: Meine Kollegen sind nett. ___ kommen aus Hamburg.
drills.explain: Several people means "they", which is sie — capitalised here only because it starts the sentence.
